Sure! Here's the recipe for marinated cheese with onions:

Ingredients:
- 1 pound of cheese (any hard cheese that you like)
- 2 finely diced onions
- 1/2 cup of vinegar
- 1/4 cup of oil
- 2 tablespoons of sugar
- 1 teaspoon of salt
- 1/4 teaspoon of pepper
- 1/2 teaspoon of caraway seeds (optional)

Instructions:
1. Cut the cheese in half, crosswise, then place it in a shallow bowl. 2. In a separate bowl, mix together the onions, vinegar, sugar, salt, pepper, and caraway seeds (if using). 3. Let the mixture sit for a few minutes until the salt has dissolved. 4. Add the oil and stir everything together. 5. Pour the mixture over the cheese, making sure that it is evenly covered. 6. Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and refrigerate for 1 to 2 days, turning the cheese occasionally, until it is fully marinated. 7. Serve the cheese with the onions, as well as dark bread and butter. Enjoy your marinated cheese with onions!<|im_end|>

Pitching a camping hammock tarp is essential to enjoy a comfortable and secure camping experience. Not only does it offer the right amount of shelter and shade, but it also keeps the harsh weather conditions at bay. Here is a comprehensive step-by-step guide on how to pitch your camping hammock tarp to offer the maximum amount of protection.

Things you’ll need:

• Tarp

• Hammock

• Tent or tent stakes

• Ropes

• Tree straps

Step 1: Choose the right spot

The ideal location to pitch a camping hammock tarp should be on an elevated terrain, free from any rocks, debris, or uneven surfaces. The ground should be soft enough to drive the tent stakes into the ground without much struggle. If you’re pitching near trees, make sure the branches aren't too low, too thick or too feeble.

Step 2: Anchor the tarp

Start by laying out the tarp on the ground and attaching the ropes to each of its four corners after folding it diagonally. Ensure that you pull each rope outwards to create a slight tension before you anchor them to the ground using tent stakes.

Step 3: Adjust the height

Before you adjust the height of your tarp, ensure that you place your hammock below the tarp's center. Use your adjustable tree straps to suspend your hammock between the two trees, placing it directly below the center of the tarp.

Step 4: Tighten the ropes

Now that you have anchored the tarp in place and adjusted its height, it's time to tighten its ropes. You can do this by pulling each rope until there is enough tension, so there's no slack left in the ropes. Use a taut-line hitch knot to keep the ropes taught/secure and ensure that the tarp is taut.

Step 5: Create a drip line

Take small branches, straps, or even trekking poles and create a drip line for the water to run off your tarp. Place the drip line on top of your tarp and tie them to the main ropes. This will help extend the life of your tarp by preventing water pooling.

Step 6: Secure the guy lines

The final step is to secure the guy lines. Take the excess rope and secure each one to an adjacent tree or use stakes to anchor them to the ground. Keep the tension right so that the tarp remains taut all through.

Everyone knows that butterflies come from caterpillars, right?
Dive into this fully-illustrated account of her life: bursting with art, history and juicy details.
1869 is considered as the year of discovery of the Periodic System by Dmitri Mendeleev. 2019 will be the 150th anniversary of the Periodic Table of Chemical Elements and has therefore been proclaimed the “International Year of the Periodic Table of Chemical Elements (IYPT2019)” by the United Nations General Assembly and UNESCO.
Every fall, spectacular orange and black clouds of monarch butterflies fill the skies as they migrate from across North America to Central Mexico. West Coast populations make a similar though much shorter trip to coastal California. The National Wildlife Federation calls the monarch migration “one of the greatest natural phenomena in the insect world.” Not long ago, monarchs numbered in the billions, but in the last 20 years their population has dropped by 90%, due to habitat loss from pesticides, modern farming practices, urban development and other human activity. An estimated one million acres of habitat are lost each year.
But today, an army of citizen scientists, students and gardeners is engaged in restoring this beloved pollinator’s habitat – the wildflowers and milkweed and feeding corridors – so that one of nature’s most beautiful creatures will still be there for generations to come. And it starts in our own backyards.
The Monarch showcases this magnificent butterfly with eye-popping photos, fun facts about a monarch’s life cycle, and things to know about the vital role that pollinators play in our ecosystem. Monarch enthusiast and nature blogger Kylee Baumle provides “action” projects for all ages, from planting milkweed and wildflowers to making butterfly watering stations…to volunteer activism.
A history of weather reporting and the naming of clouds is brought to life in an examination of the young life of Luke Howard, who as a young boy kept a weather journal and eventually created a system for naming clouds which, in a modified form, is still used today. - 2 cups heavy cream
- 1 cup whole milk
- 3/4 cup honey
- 1/2 cup unsweetened cocoa powder
- 1/4 tsp salt
- 4 egg yolks
- 1 tsp vanilla extract

Instructions:
1. In a medium saucepan, heat the cream, milk, honey, cocoa powder, and salt over medium heat, whisking occasionally until well combined and hot but not boiling.
2. In a separate bowl, whisk the egg yolks until smooth.
3. Slowly pour about 1 cup of the hot chocolate mixture into the egg yolks, whisking constantly to temper the eggs.
4. Pour the egg mixture back into the saucepan with the remaining chocolate mixture, whisking constantly.
5. Cook the mixture over medium heat, stirring constantly, until it thickens and coats the back of a spoon, about 10-12 minutes.
6. Strain the mixture through a fine-mesh sieve into a clean bowl.
7. Stir in the vanilla extract.
8. Cover the bowl and chill the mixture in the refrigerator for at least 4 hours or overnight.
